destination.title: The Hidden Code Door Behind the $8 Billion FTX Fraud

short04: A crypto exchange was holding billions of its customers' dollars.
Then about eight billion of it went missing.
FTX was one of the biggest crypto exchanges in the world, and its founder was its most trusted face.
But hidden in the code was a secret exception.
A private trading firm could pull customer deposits almost without limit.
When everyone asked for their money back, it wasn't there.
In 2023, a jury found the founder guilty in one of the largest frauds in U.S.
Even in crypto, spending customers' money is theft.
Watch the full story on the channel.

candidate_payload_lines: concrete shareable details (shorts + video games, Super Bowl ad, arena, $26B→0); a clearly illustrative victim beat; quotable hard lines ("It isn't 'crypto.' It's theft."); stronger emotional verdict payoff.
The wall between "money we're holding for customers" and "money we're gambling with" — that wall *was* the promise.
But "you'll get most of it back, years later, if you fight through a court" is not what the ad promised.
Endorsers/non-defendants never implied to be part of the fraud.
To understand how eight billion dollars walks out the door, you have to understand why nobody was watching it.
To keep pulling money out after it hit zero.
As long as everyone didn't ask for their money back at the same time, no one would ever see the door.
On November 2nd, 2023, the jury went out.
On March 28th, 2024, the judge sentenced him to twenty-five years in federal prison and ordered him to forfeit more than eleven billion dollars.
era_note: SET THIS. Modern stock footage is only usable if the case is modern; a 1960s case dressed in present-day footage reads wrong.

shorts.angle: The week a million people asked for their money back at the same time, and the exchange could not hand it over.
shorts.type: B - the run, and the size of the hole it exposed
shorts.avoids: short04 explains the hidden code exception and the guilty verdict. It never covers the run itself, how fast the fortune evaporated, or the exact shape of what was owed.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: The money was not set on fire. So where did eight billion dollars actually go?

lines.text: November 2022. Customers start doing the one thing the hidden door cannot survive. They ask for their money back. All of them. At once.
source_lines: a rival pulls its support, and customers start doing the one thing the hidden door cannot survive
They ask for their money back. All of them. At once.

lines.text: In days, customers try to yank billions off the exchange. A healthy company just hands it over. It is your money. It is right there.
source_lines: In days, customers try to yank billions off the exchange.
A healthy company just hands it over. It's your money. It's right there.

lines.text: FTX couldn't. Most of what customers thought was sitting safely on the exchange wasn't there anymore.
source_lines: FTX couldn't. Because most of what customers thought was sitting safely on the exchange wasn't there anymore.

lines.text: By some estimates his wealth fell from around sixteen billion dollars to under one billion in a single day. Within days, effectively zero.
source_lines: By some estimates, Bankman-Fried's wealth fell from around sixteen billion dollars to under one billion — in a single day.
Within days, effectively zero.

lines.text: Three in the morning, somewhere in America. A customer opens the app, stares at his life savings, and taps withdraw. Nothing happens.
source_lines: It's 3 a.m. Somewhere in America, a man opens an app and stares at a number — his life savings.
He taps "withdraw." Nothing happens. It will never happen.

lines.text: Beyond the customers, about 1.7 billion dollars was owed to investors and another 1.3 billion to Alameda's lenders. FTX filed for bankruptcy.
source_lines: About 1.7 billion to investors.
Another 1.3 billion to Alameda's lenders.
FTX filed for bankruptcy.

lines.text: A run is the oldest test there is. The hidden door stayed invisible only while the deposits sat where customers believed they were.
source_lines: It's the oldest test there is — a run.
As long as everyone didn't ask for their money back at the same time, no one would ever see the door.

lines.text: Roughly eight billion owed to customers. It was not burned. It was moved, bet and spent, long before anyone asked for it back.

shorts.loop_join: L5 stops on the money being gone before anyone asked for it, and L1 picks up with the asking: they all want it back at once.

shorts.angle: The witnesses who ended him were not investigators. They were the people who built the thing with him.
shorts.type: C - the testimony, and the sentence that followed
shorts.avoids: short04 states that a jury found him guilty and stops there. It never says who testified, what they said, or what the sentence and forfeiture actually were.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: Twenty-five years for an eight-billion-dollar fraud. Too much, too little, or exactly right?

lines.text: His defense, boiled down: mistakes were made, but not crimes.
source_lines: His defense, boiled down: mistakes were made — but not crimes.

lines.text: The problem was who sat in the witness chair. Not outside investigators. His own inner circle.
source_lines: The problem was who sat in the witness chair. Not outside investigators — his own inner circle.

lines.text: The co-founder who built the code with him described, out loud, the secret setting that let the money move. They testified the use of customer money was no accident.
source_lines: The co-founder who built the code with him and described, out loud, the secret setting that let the money move.
They testified the use of customer money was no accident.

lines.text: On November 2nd, 2023, the jury went out. It was back in a few hours. Guilty on all seven counts. Wire fraud, conspiracy, money laundering.
source_lines: On November 2nd, 2023, the jury went out. It was back in a few hours.
On all seven counts — wire fraud, conspiracy, money laundering.

lines.text: Prosecutors called it one of the biggest financial frauds in American history. FTX was bankrupt, and the arena scrubbed its name off the building.
source_lines: Prosecutors called it one of the biggest financial frauds in American history.
FTX filed for bankruptcy.
The arena that carried his company's name? They scrubbed it off the building.

lines.text: Through years of bankruptcy proceedings much of the money was eventually clawed back for customers, years later, by fighting through a court.
source_lines: The money was moved, bet, and spent — and through years of bankruptcy proceedings, much of it was eventually clawed back for customers.
But "you'll get most of it back, years later, if you fight through a court" is not what the ad promised.

lines.text: To the million customers, the balance on the screen was real. On the night it mattered, it was a ghost.
source_lines: FTX made that promise to a million customers.
To them, the balance on the screen was real.
On the night it mattered, it was a ghost.

lines.text: The jury did not buy it. Twenty-five years in federal prison, and an order to forfeit more than eleven billion dollars.
